pos: n. (Johann Walter, 1496–1570, cantor of Torgau and first musician of the Lutheran Reformation)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Walter, ruler of the army.
biblical_def: Johann Walter was a singer in the Saxon court chapel who spent three weeks in Luther's house in 1524 helping him fit German words to music, and who then published the first evangelical hymnbook with parts, the Geystliche gesangk Buchleyn of that year. Luther wrote the preface. Walter went on to be cantor at Torgau, where he founded the town choir, and later organised the chapel of the elector at Dresden; he set the German Mass, the Passions, and a great deal besides. He is the man who decided what the Reformation would sound like. His settings keep the melody in the tenor with the other voices around it, so that a congregation singing the tune can be carried by a trained choir without being replaced by it, and that arrangement is a theological decision as much as a musical one. The people sing. The choir helps them. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cantor as a singer, one who leads in church music, and chorale as a hymn tune of plain and slow movement.
webster_full: CANT'OR, n. A singer; a leader of the music in a church or chapel.
CHOIR, n. A collection of singers, especially in divine service; the part of a church appropriated to the singers.
HAR'MONY, n. In music, the accordance of two or more sounds; a succession of chords according to the rules of composition.
TEN'OR, n. In music, the natural pitch of a man's voice; the part which holds the principal melody.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
corruption_summary: The cantor who decided what the Reformation would sound like, with the tune in the people's part.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse concerns the relation between a choir and a congregation, and it has gone wrong in both directions since. A choir that performs while the people listen has turned worship into a concert; a congregation that will admit no trained singing at all has thrown away a help Scripture plainly contemplates, since the temple had appointed singers. Walter's solution keeps both in their places by putting the melody where the people can hold it.

The principle to recover is that congregational singing is commanded as mutual teaching and therefore must be singable by the taught. “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). Paul then adds the requirement that governs every musical decision in a church: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also” (1Co 14:15). Understanding is not optional, and it is the first casualty when the music outruns the people.

pos: n. (Paul Speratus, 1484–1551, hymnwriter and Lutheran bishop of Pomesania)
etymology: Latin Paulus, little; Speratus, hoped for, from sperare, to hope.
biblical_def: Paul Speratus preached against clerical celibacy and monastic vows in Vienna cathedral in 1522, was excommunicated for it, went to Moravia, was imprisoned at Olmütz under sentence of death, and wrote in that prison the hymn that put the doctrine of justification into German verse: fourteen stanzas beginning with the declaration that salvation has come to us by grace and sheer goodness, and that works will never help, since they cannot protect. It went into the first evangelical hymnbook of 1524 alongside Luther's own, and three of the eight hymns in that little volume are Speratus's. He was released, worked with Luther at Wittenberg, and ended as Lutheran bishop of Pomesania in Prussia. The hymn is the thing. A man under sentence of death wrote fourteen verses of catechesis on grace and works, and a generation of Germans learned the doctrine by singing them. That is the Reformation's most effective instrument and it was forged in a cell. “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stanza as a number of lines connected with each other, and celibacy as an unmarried state, single life.
webster_full: STAN'ZA, n. In poetry, a number of lines or verses connected with each other, and ending in a full point or pause.
CEL'IBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a promise by which a person binds himself to an act or service.
DUN'GEON, n. A close prison, or a deep dark place of confinement.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
corruption_summary: Fourteen stanzas on grace and works, written in a cell under sentence of death.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the relegation of hymnody to the expression of feeling, with the result that a congregation's songs carry no doctrine and the people learn nothing by singing. Speratus wrote fourteen stanzas of argument. The hymn states the problem, states the false solution, states the remedy, and applies it, and it does all this in verse a farmer could sing from memory in a field.

The principle to recover is that what Scripture says about grace and works is precise and can be stated in a sentence, which is why it is singable at all. “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and then the clause that shuts the door: “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). And the setting of the hymn's composition is itself apostolic: “at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them” (Act 16:25).

pos: n. (Nikolaus Decius, c. 1485–c. 1546, monk turned hymnwriter, author of the German Gloria)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; Latin Decius, a latinised form of the surname Tech or Deeg.
biblical_def: Nikolaus Decius was prior of a convent in Brunswick who left it in 1522, taught at Brunswick, and became a preacher at Stettin and afterwards in East Frisia. He turned two of the fixed parts of the Latin mass into German hymns that the whole congregation could sing: the Gloria in excelsis became a hymn of praise to God alone in the highest, and the Agnus Dei became a hymn to the Lamb of God who bears the sin of the world. He is said to have composed the tunes as well as the words, adapting old plainsong. The significance of this is easy to miss at four and a half centuries. Those two texts were the choir's property and were sung in a language the people did not know; Decius put them into German verse with a singable tune, and the congregation got them back. Nothing was added and nothing was subtracted. What changed is who was allowed to sing. “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (Joh 1:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Gloria as a doxology or hymn of praise, and plainsong as the simple unmeasured chant of the ancient church.
webster_full: DOXOL'OGY, n. In Christian worship, a hymn in praise of the Almighty; a particular form of giving glory to God.
CHANT, n. Song; melody; a kind of sacred music in which the words are recited on a reciting note.
VER'NACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth.
LITURGY, n. A formulary of public devotions; the established formulas of public worship.
scriptures: Joh 1:29
The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
Luk 2:14
Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
Rev 5:9

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;
corruption_summary: The Gloria and the Agnus Dei given back to the congregation in German.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that putting the liturgy into the common tongue was a lowering of worship, a trade of beauty for accessibility. Decius took texts the choir had sung in Latin, kept their words, adapted their melodies, and gave them to the people in German. The beauty was not spent; the ownership changed.

The principle to recover is that intelligibility in public worship is an apostolic requirement and not a modern convenience, and Paul puts a ratio on it that leaves no argument: “Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19). The song of the redeemed is sung by people out of every tongue (Rev 5:9), and what they sing is the confession the Baptist made at the Jordan: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (Joh 1:29).

pos: n. (Elisabeth Cruciger, c. 1500–1535, the first woman hymnwriter of the Reformation)
etymology: Hebrew Elisheba, God is an oath, God is my fulness; Latin Cruciger, cross-bearer.
biblical_def: Elisabeth Cruciger was a Pomeranian noblewoman who left the convent at Treptow, came to Wittenberg, and in 1524 married Caspar Cruciger, one of Luther's colleagues. In the same year a hymn of hers appeared in the earliest evangelical hymnbooks: five stanzas on the eternal Son, the Father's only-begotten, the morning star risen above all others, with a prayer that he would make his light shine in the singer and give strength to run the course. It is a hymn on the person of Christ, dense and precise, and it stood in the German books for four hundred years. She died at about thirty-five and almost nothing else of hers survives. Later editors, uneasy at a woman's name in the hymnbook, tried at various times to reassign the hymn to Andreas Knopken or to a Bohemian source; the contemporary attributions are to her. She did not preach, hold office or teach publicly. She wrote five stanzas in her own house and the church sang them for four centuries. “I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines only-begotten as the only son, sole begotten, and morning star as the planet Venus when it precedes the sun.
webster_full: BEGOT'TEN, participle passive. Procreated; generated; as the only begotten Son of God.
MORN'ING-STAR, n. The planet Venus, when it rises before the sun; used figuratively of a harbinger.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God.
ATTRIBU'TION, n. The act of attributing; the ascribing to one of a quality, character or work.
scriptures: I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: Five stanzas on the eternal Son, sung in the German churches for four hundred years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite misuses attach to this entry. The first is the old editorial embarrassment that tried to take the hymn away from her and give it to a man, which the sources do not support. The second is the modern enlistment of her as a frustrated preacher, which the record supports no better: she wrote a hymn in her own house, she held no office, she sought none, and the church received what she gave.

The principle to recover is that the apostolic charge to sing doctrine to one another is laid on the whole congregation without distinction of sex. “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16) is written to a church, and a hymn a woman writes and the church sings is that verse obeyed, not a boundary crossed. The subject she chose is the highest there is: “the glory as of the only begotten of the Father” (Joh 1:14).

pos: n. (Philipp Nicolai, 1556–1608, Lutheran pastor and hymnwriter of Unna and Hamburg)
etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; Latin Nicolai, of Nicolaus, victory of the people.
biblical_def: Philipp Nicolai was pastor at Unna in Westphalia in 1597 when the plague came and killed some thirteen hundred of his people in six months. He buried as many as thirty in a day; his own house looked out on the churchyard. In that year he wrote a book of meditations on eternal life for the survivors, and appended to it two hymns that became the king and queen of the German chorales — one on the morning star and the love of the bridegroom for his soul, one a watchman's call at midnight summoning the wise virgins to meet him. Both are wedding songs. A man burying his parish wrote two hymns about a marriage feast, and he wrote them for the people still alive in the houses around the churchyard. Nothing explains the Reformation's hymnody better than that. The eschatology is not an escape from the plague; it is the answer to it. “And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him” (Mat 25:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pestilence as a plague or malignant disease, and bridegroom as a man newly married or about to be married.
webster_full: PES'TILENCE, n. Plague, appropriately so called; but in a general sense, any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.
BRI'DEGROOM, n. A man newly married, or who is about to be married.
MEDITA'TION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind.
CHORAL, a. Belonging to or composed for a choir or concert; singing in a choir.
scriptures: Mat 25:6
And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.
Rev 19:7
Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.
I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: Two wedding hymns written by a pastor burying thirty of his people a day.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of treating the church's last things as a specialist interest or an embarrassment, so that a congregation under real affliction is offered comfort drawn from anywhere except the one place the New Testament puts it. Nicolai's parish was dying around him and he gave them the marriage supper of the Lamb, set to a tune they could sing.

The principle to recover is that the Lord's own picture of the end is a wedding and a summons given at midnight, which is to say at the worst hour. “And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him” (Mat 25:6). John hears the same thing as a shout of gladness: “the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready” (Rev 19:7). Against thirteen hundred graves, the psalmist's verdict stands: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15).

pos: n. (Martin Rinkart, 1586–1649, archdeacon of Eilenburg and hymnwriter of the Thirty Years' War)
etymology: Latin Martinus, of Mars, warlike; German Rinkart, from a Saxon surname.
biblical_def: Martin Rinkart was archdeacon of Eilenburg in Saxony through the whole of the Thirty Years' War. The town was walled, so refugees crowded into it; plague followed, then famine, then the Swedes. In 1637 the other clergy were dead or fled and Rinkart buried the dead of the town almost alone, something near four thousand of them in that year, including his wife. He is said to have gone out and persuaded a Swedish commander to reduce a crushing levy on the starving town. Out of those years came a short table grace in three stanzas for his children, calling on all to give thanks to God with heart and hands and voices, which has since become the thanksgiving hymn of the German-speaking world and of much of the English-speaking one. It is a grace before meat, written in a town with no food, by a man who had buried his wife and most of his parish. “In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you” (1Th 5:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thanksgiving as the act of rendering thanks for favors received, and famine as scarcity of food, dearth.
webster_full: THANKSGIV'ING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
FAM'INE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
ARCH'DEACON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.
LEVY, n. The act of raising money or troops; a tax or imposition.
scriptures: In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
Hab 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Hab 3:18
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
Job 1:21
And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
corruption_summary: A table grace in three stanzas, written in a starving town by a man who buried four thousand.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reduction of thanksgiving to a response proportioned to circumstances, so that gratitude is what a comfortable people produce and lament is what everyone else gets. Rinkart's hymn refutes the arrangement by existing. It was written as a grace before meat in a town with no meat, by a man burying his neighbours at a rate of ten a day.

The principle to recover is that the command is unqualified and the reason given is the will of God rather than the state of the table: “In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you” (1Th 5:18). Habakkuk works through the entire inventory of loss and then turns on one word: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (Hab 3:18). Job says the same at the graveside of his children: “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21).

Greek thelema (G2307) — will, determination, purpose; 1 Thessalonians 5:18.

pos: n. (Georg Neumark, 1621–1681, German poet, librarian at Weimar and hymnwriter)
etymology: Greek Georgios, a husbandman; German Neumark, the new march or borderland.
biblical_def: Georg Neumark was robbed of everything he had on the road to university in 1641, wandered destitute for months through a Germany ruined by war, and was at the point of despair in Kiel when a pastor got him a place as a tutor in a household. He wrote his hymn that day, and he wrote in his own account that he did it out of a heart so full of thankfulness that he had to put it somewhere. Seven stanzas: let him who lets God govern him and hopes in him at all times be kept wonderfully in every cross and sadness, for whoever trusts God has not built on sand. Neumark later became librarian and secretary at the court of Weimar and wrote a great deal more that nobody reads. The one hymn from the worst day of his life has been sung in German and English for three and a half centuries. “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” (Psa 55:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sustain as to bear, to support, to keep from sinking, and destitute as needy, abject, comfortless.
webster_full: SUSTA'IN, v. To bear; to uphold; to support; to keep from sinking in ruin.
DES'TITUTE, a. Needy; abject; comfortless; friendless; wanting necessaries.
PROV'IDENCE, n. In theology, the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
LI'BRARIAN, n. The keeper or one who has the care of a library.
scriptures: Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
Mat 7:26
And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:
corruption_summary: Seven stanzas written on the day a destitute student was given a place.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern reading of trust in providence as passivity, a refusal to act dressed up as faith. Neumark's hymn was written by a man who had walked across a ruined country looking for work and had just been given some. The trust in it is not a substitute for the walking; it is what the walking was done in.

The principle to recover is that casting a burden is an act, and Scripture commands it in the imperative with the ground attached. “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee” (Psa 55:22). Peter gives the reason that makes the command bearable: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7). And the hymn's closing image is the Lord's own, the two builders and the two foundations: “built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24).

“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7) — seven stanzas in one day.
“built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24) — whoever trusts God has not built on sand.

pos: n. (Johann Heermann, 1585–1647, Silesian pastor and hymnwriter)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Heermann, an army man, from Heer, an army.
biblical_def: Johann Heermann was pastor at Köben on the Oder through the Thirty Years' War, in a town that was plundered four times, burned, and swept by plague; he lost his property repeatedly, nearly lost his life, and from 1634 lost his voice and could no longer preach. He wrote hymns instead, something over four hundred, and the best of them are among the finest in the German language. The greatest is a passion hymn asking what law the blessed Lord has broken, that so sharp a sentence should be passed on him, and answering across its fifteen stanzas that the guilt was the singer's own and the stripes were his. Heermann is the hinge between the objective chorale of the Reformation and the more personal hymnody that followed; the doctrine in him is as hard as Luther's and the address is to the singer's own conscience. A man who could not speak wrote the German church's passion hymn. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines passion as the sufferings of Christ, and stripe as a blow with a lash, a wound made by a scourge.
webster_full: PAS'SION, n. The last suffering of the Savior; the sufferings of Christ in the garden and on the cross.
STRIPE, n. A stroke made with a lash, whip, rod or scourge; a wound made by a lash.
PLUN'DER, v. To pillage; to spoil; to strip of goods by open force.
CHO'RALE, n. A hymn tune of plain and slow movement, sung by a congregation.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Isa 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
corruption_summary: Four hundred hymns from a plundered town, written after the pastor lost his voice.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentimental passion hymn, which dwells on the physical suffering and leaves the singer as a spectator moved by a cruelty. Heermann's hymn refuses that from its first line: it asks what the Lord has done to deserve the sentence, and the answer it works out over fifteen stanzas is that he did nothing and the singer did everything, and that the transfer was deliberate.

The principle to recover is substitution stated in the prophet's own prepositions. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5). The exchange is then made explicit: “the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa 53:6). Paul states both directions of it in one sentence: “he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21).
roots_summary: Hebrew chalal (H2490), to pierce, to wound; chaburah (H2250), a stripe, a bruise.

Hebrew daka (H1792) — to crush, to bruise, to break in pieces; Isaiah 53:5.
Hebrew chaburah (H2250) — a stripe, a bruise, a wound; Isaiah 53:5.
Hebrew paga (H6293) — to light upon, to cause to fall upon; Isaiah 53:6.
Greek anaphero (G399) — to carry up, to bear; 1 Peter 2:24.
usage: “he was wounded for our transgressions” (Isa 53:5) — the German passion hymn, fifteen stanzas.
“the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa 53:6) — Köben, plundered four times.
“he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin” (2Co 5:21) — written after he lost his voice.

pos: n. (Johann Crüger, 1598–1662, cantor of St Nicholas in Berlin and composer of chorale tunes)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Crüger, a potter, from Krug, a jug.
biblical_def: Johann Crüger was cantor of the Nikolaikirche in Berlin for forty years and the man who gave the German chorale most of the tunes it is still sung to. He set Rinkart's thanksgiving, Heermann's passion hymn, and a long list of Paul Gerhardt's texts; Gerhardt was his pastor at St Nicholas and the two worked together for years, which is as fruitful a partnership between a poet and a composer as the church has had. Crüger's hymnbook of 1640 and its many enlarged editions carried these tunes across Germany. His melodies are plain, strong, and pitched for ordinary voices, and he harmonised them with a figured bass so that a household with one instrument could sing them at home as well as a church could. He was also a theorist and wrote on music. The tune is not a vehicle for the words; a bad tune buries a good hymn and a good tune carries a congregation for four centuries. The psalm asks for skill by name: “Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise” (Psa 33:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines melody as an agreeable succession of sounds, and skilful as knowing, well versed in any art.
webster_full: MEL'ODY, n. An agreeable succession of sounds; a succession of sounds so regulated and modulated as to please the ear.
SKIL'FUL, a. Knowing; well versed in any art; hence, dextrous; able in management.
COM'POSER, n. An author; one who composes or writes music.
CAN'TOR, n. A singer; a leader of the music in a church or chapel.
scriptures: Psa 33:3
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
Praise ye the LORD: for it is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Psa 98:1
A Psalm. O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory.
corruption_summary: Forty years at St Nicholas, and the tunes the German chorale is still sung to.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the treatment of the tune as a neutral container for the text, so that a hymn's music may be changed at pleasure and nothing is lost. Four centuries of singing say otherwise. Crüger's settings are why Rinkart, Heermann and Gerhardt are sung at all; a different cantor would have given the German church a different memory.

The principle to recover is that Scripture asks for skill in this and does not treat it as an indulgence. “Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise” (Psa 33:3) is a command with a standard inside it, and David appointed a Levite over the song of the house on exactly that ground. The praise itself is pronounced fitting: “it is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely” (Psa 147:1). A tune that a congregation can carry is part of what that verse asks for.
roots_summary: Hebrew yatab (H3190), to do a thing well, to play skilfully; naveh (H5000), comely, seemly.
roots_lines: Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to make good, to do well, to play skilfully; Psalm 33:3.
Hebrew nagan (H5059) — to touch strings, to play an instrument; Psalm 33:3.
Hebrew naveh (H5000) — comely, becoming, seemly; Psalm 147:1.
Greek psallo (G5567) — to make melody, to sing a psalm; Ephesians 5:19.
Hebrew chadash (H2319) — new, fresh, recent; Psalm 98:1.
usage: “play skilfully with a loud noise” (Psa 33:3) — the Berlin hymnbook of 1640.
“praise is comely” (Psa 147:1) — the tunes for Rinkart, Heermann and Gerhardt.
“O sing unto the LORD a new song” (Psa 98:1) — forty years as cantor at St Nicholas.

pos: n. (William Kethe, d. c. 1594, Scottish or English exile, psalm versifier of the Geneva psalter)
etymology: Germanic William, resolute protector; Kethe, probably from a Scottish surname.
biblical_def: William Kethe was a Marian exile, probably a Scot, who settled at Geneva and worked on the English metrical psalter there. Twenty-five of his versions went into the Anglo-Genevan psalter of 1561, and one of them has outlived everything else in the book: the hundredth psalm in long metre, calling all people that on earth do dwell to sing to the Lord with cheerful voice, set to the tune that has been called Old Hundredth ever since. It is sung every week in more churches than any other psalm version in English. Kethe afterwards went back to England, held a living in Dorset, and served as an army chaplain in two campaigns. Almost nothing else is known of him, including where he was born. The man is a blank and the psalm is everywhere, which is not a bad proportion for a servant of the church and is very nearly the rule in hymnody. “Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing” (Psa 100:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines metre as the arrangement of poetical feet or syllables in verse, and version as a translation, that which is rendered from another language.
webster_full: ME'TRE, n. The arrangement of poetical feet, or of long and short syllables in verse.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition in verse, to be sung in divine worship.
PSALT'ER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
scriptures: Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.
A Psalm of praise. Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands.
Psa 95:1
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
Psa 30:4
Sing unto the LORD, O ye saints of his, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.
corruption_summary: Twenty-five psalm versions, of which the hundredth is sung every week in half the world.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a quiet contempt for metrical psalmody as a crude expedient of an unmusical age, superseded once the churches had real hymns. The hundredth psalm in Kethe's version answers the charge by being better than most of what replaced it, and the principle behind the psalter answers it more completely: a congregation that sings the psalms is singing words God gave them, in their own tongue, in a shape they can carry.

The principle to recover is that the psalm itself commands the manner as well as the act. “Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing” (Psa 100:2). Gladness is specified and so is singing, and the summons is to all the earth: “Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands” (Psa 100:1). The saints are addressed by name for the same duty: “Sing unto the LORD, O ye saints of his” (Psa 30:4).
roots_summary: Hebrew simchah (H8057), gladness, joy, mirth; renanah (H7445), a ringing cry, singing.
roots_lines: Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, to serve, to labour; Psalm 100:2.
Hebrew simchah (H8057) — gladness, joy, mirth; Psalm 100:2.
Hebrew renanah (H7445) — a ringing cry, a shout of joy, singing; Psalm 100:2.
Hebrew ruwa (H7321) — to shout, to raise a war-cry or a shout of joy; Psalm 100:1.
Hebrew zamar (H2167) — to make music, to sing praise; Psalm 30:4.
usage: “Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing” (Psa 100:2) — Geneva, 1561.
“Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands” (Psa 100:1) — the Old Hundredth.
“Sing unto the LORD, O ye saints of his” (Psa 30:4) — twenty-five versions in the psalter.
